title: Corrigendum to: Computing Optimal Ate Pairings on Elliptic   Curves with Embedding Degree 9, 15 and 27
abstract:
We correct two errors in Section~8 of the above-mentioned paper
concerning the seed parameters proposed for BLS27 elliptic curves
(embedding degree $k=27$) at the $256$-bit and $192$-bit security levels.
In both instances, the disclosed seeds produce a composite $r(x)$,
violating the primality condition essential for constructing
pairing-friendly curves. Additionally, for the $192$-bit seed the
characteristic $p(x)$ is also composite. We provide verified corrected
seeds for each security level, obtained by exhaustive search, and confirm
with SageMath that both $p(x)$ and $r(x)$ are prime in each case.
All other results of the original paper remain valid.

Corrigendum to: Computing Optimal Ate Pairings on Elliptic Curves with Embedding
                             Degree 9, 15 and 27
          Journal of Groups, Complexity, Cryptology, Vol. 12, Issue 1, 2020, pp. 3:1–3:25

                            Walid Haddaji: haddajiwalid95@gmail.com

                                                June 8, 2026


                                                   Abstract
            We correct two errors in Section 8 of the above-mentioned paper concerning the seed
        parameters proposed for BLS27 elliptic curves (embedding degree k = 27) at the 256-bit and
        192-bit security levels. In both instances, the disclosed seeds produce a composite r(x), vio-
        lating the primality condition essential for constructing pairing-friendly curves. Additionally,
        for the 192-bit seed the characteristic p(x) is also composite. We provide verified corrected
        seeds for each security level, obtained by exhaustive search, and confirm with SageMath that
        both p(x) and r(x) are prime in each case. All other results of the original paper remain
        valid.

Keywords: BLS27 curves, pairing friendly curves, bilinear pairings, seed correction, SageMath.


1.      Background and Notation
The BLS27 family of pairing-friendly elliptic curves [2] is parametrised by an integer x via the
polynomials

                            p(x) = 13 (x − 1)2 x18 + x9 + 1 + x,
                                                             
                                                                                             (1)
                            r(x) = 31 x18 + x9 + 1 ,
                                                    
                                                                                             (2)
                                   t(x) = x + 1,                                                           (3)

where p is the characteristic of the base field, r is the order of the pairing-friendly subgroup, and
t is the Frobenius trace [6]. For the curve E/Fp defined by these polynomials to yield a valid
pairing-friendly instance it is necessary that:

     1. p(x) is prime (the base field characteristic);

     2. r(x) is prime (the subgroup order);

     3. x ≡ 1 (mod 3) so that 3 | (x18 + x9 + 1) and r(x) is an integer.

A composite r(x) admits small-subgroup attacks [8] and invalidates the hardness assumption
underlying every pairing-based protocol built on the curve [3, 4].
For resistance against the SexTNFS discrete-logarithm algorithm, Barbulescu–Duquesne [1] and
Scott–Guillevic [9] require log2 (p27 ) ≥ 27 410 at the AES-256 level and log2 (p27 ) ≥ 12 871 at
the AES-192 level (Table 4 of [5]). Since deg p = 20 and deg r = 18 in x, one has log2 p ≈
(20/18) log2 r (the ρ-value is 10/9).
Throughout, M1 , S1 , I1 denote the costs of a multiplication, squaring and inversion in Fp , and
Icyc denotes inversion in the relevant cyclotomic subgroup, following the notation of [5].

2.    Error at the 256-Bit Security Level (Section 8.3)
In Section 8.3 of [5], the seed proposed for the 256-bit security level is
                                     (256)
                                xold         = 251 + 242 + 228 + 29 + 1.                   (4)
                         
                    (256)                             (256)
Proposition 1. r xold        is composite. Hence xold does not define a valid pairing-friendly
                                    
                               (256)
curve. The characteristic p xold       is, however, prime.

Proof. The following SageMath [10] session verifies both claims:
sage: x0 = 2^51 + 2^42 + 2^28 + 2^9 + 1
sage: R.<x> = ZZ[]
sage: r = (x^18 + x^9 + 1) // 3
sage: p = ((x-1)^2*(x^18+x^9+1))//3 + x
sage: r(x0).is_prime()
False
sage: p(x0).is_prime()
True


Corrected seed. We replace (4) with

                             x(256)  51  39  33  25  6
                              new = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1.                                 (5)
                             (256)
Proposition 2. The seed xnew defined by (5) is valid. Specifically:
             
        (256)
 (i) r xnew is a prime of 917 bits;
              
         (256)
 (ii) p xnew is a prime of 1019 bits;

(iii) log2 p27 = 27 513 ≥ 27 410, satisfying the SexTNFS resistance bound of [1, 9];
              

       (256)
 (iv) xnew ≡ 1 (mod 3);
                                (256)                                  (256)
 (v) The Hamming weight of xnew is 6, one more than that of xold , resulting in one additional
     addition step in the Miller loop.

Proof. sage: x_new = 2^51 + 2^39 + 2^33 + 2^25 + 2^6 + 1
sage: r(x_new).is_prime(), p(x_new).is_prime()
(True, True)
sage: r(x_new).nbits(), p(x_new).nbits()
(917, 1019)
sage: 27 * p(x_new).nbits()
27513
sage: x_new % 3
1
sage: bin(x_new).count(’1’)
6

3.    Error at the 192-Bit Security Level (Section 8.2)
In Section 8.2 of [5], the seed proposed for the 192-bit security level is
                                     (192)
                             xold = 225 + 217 + 214 + 24 + 1.                               (6)
                                         
                       (192)          (192)
Proposition 3. Both r xold     and p xold     are composite.

Proof. sage: x1 = 2^25 + 2^17 + 2^14 + 2^4 + 1
sage: r(x1).is_prime(), p(x1).is_prime()
(False, False)


Corrected seed. We replace (6) with

                                x(192)  24  23  20  11
                                 new = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1.                                   (7)

This corrected seed was previously presented in [7].
                             (192)
Proposition 4. The seed xnew defined by (7) is valid. Specifically:
             
        (192)
 (i) r xnew is a prime of 443 bits;
              
         (192)
 (ii) p xnew is a prime of 492 bits;

(iii) log2 p27 = 13 284 ≥ 12 871, satisfying the SexTNFS resistance bound of [1, 9];
              

       (192)
 (iv) xnew ≡ 1 (mod 3);
                                 (192)                            (192)
 (v) The Hamming weight of xnew is 5, the same as that of xold .

Proof. sage: x_new2 = 2^24 + 2^23 + 2^20 + 2^11 + 1
sage: r(x_new2).is_prime(), p(x_new2).is_prime()
(True, True)
sage: r(x_new2).nbits(), p(x_new2).nbits()
(443, 492)
sage: 27 * p(x_new2).nbits()
13284
sage: x_new2 % 3
1
sage: bin(x_new2).count(’1’)
5



4.    Summary and Corrected Cost Estimates
Table 1 collects the erroneous and corrected parameter sets alongside their primality status.

Cost Corrections
Based on the corrected seeds and following the cost formulas in Sections 6 and 8 of [5], the
corrected operation counts are:

Security Level Seed x                                          log2 r log2 p log2 (p27 ) r prime p prime HW

256-bit

                225 + 217 + 214 + 24 + 1 (original)            449    499    13 473     ✗          ✗    5
192-bit
                224 + 223 + 220 + 211 + 1 (corrected)          443    492    13 284     ✓          ✓    5


                  Table 2: Corrected costs for the BLS27 optimal ate pairing.
      Level                              Miller loop                   Final exponentiation
                Original [5] (invalid)   55I1 + 21 348M1 + 9 660S1     I1 + 19 191M1 + 122 337S1
      256-bit                 (256)
                Corrected (xnew )        55I1 + 21 348M1 + 9 660S1     I1 + 19 191M1 + 122 337S1
                Original [5] (invalid)   29I1 + 11 052M1 + 4 798S1     I1 + 19 191M1 + 59 587S1
      192-bit                 (192)
                Corrected (xnew )        24I1 + 9 288M1 + 3 898S1      I1 + 17 715M1 + 55 053S1


   Remark:
                                                       (256)
  1. For the 256-bit level, the corrected seed xnew has the same leading bit (251 ) as the er-
     roneous one, so log2 r and log2 p are unchanged and the Miller loop structure (number of
     doublings and additions) is identical; the cost figures in the original paper are therefore
     correct once the seed is replaced. The Hamming weight increases from 5 to 6, adding one
     addition step, but this has negligible impact on overall cost.
  2. For the 192-bit level, the leading bit decreases from 225 to 224 , reducing the doubling count
     and yielding a modest improvement in both the Miller loop and final exponentiation costs.
   All other results, formulas, and parameter sets in [5] (for k = 9, k = 15, and the k = 27
comparison in Section 7 based on the seed of [11]) are unaffected by this corrigendum.
